title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(c)(2) Minimum Base Amount
description: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2), the base amount never falls below 50% of current-year qualified research expenses, halving the credit's marginal rate to 10%.
summary: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2), the minimum base amount rule requires that a taxpayer's base amount for the federal regular research credit never fall below 50 percent of current-year qualified research expenses. It applies to start-ups, established firms, and controlled groups alike, effectively halving the 20 percent credit's marginal rate to 10 percent before § 280C(c) adjustments.

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2), the minimum base amount rule requires that a taxpayer's base amount for the federal regular research credit never fall below 50 percent of current-year qualified research expenses. It applies to start-ups, established firms, and controlled groups alike, effectively halving the 20 percent credit's marginal rate to 10 percent before § 280C(c) adjustments.

Title 26, United States Code, Section 41(c)(2) establishes a mandatory mathematical floor for the regular federal research and development (R&D) tax credit: in no event may a taxpayer's calculated base amount be less than 50 percent of its qualified research expenses (QREs) for the credit year. Enacted as a structural safeguard within the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under 26 U.S.C. § 41, this 50 percent minimum base amount prevents rapidly scaling businesses, start-ups, or enterprises with low historical gross receipts from claiming the 20 percent regular federal credit on nearly 100 percent of their current-year research spending. By neutralizing at least half of current-year QREs whenever research expenditures grow disproportionately relative to historical revenue, § 41(c)(2) caps the portion of current-year QREs eligible for the regular credit at 50 percent and halves the nominal marginal credit rate from 20 percent to 10 percent before statutory tax-deduction adjustments under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c).

At the state level, the operational impact of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) is amplified under California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) § 23609 (for corporations) and § 17052.12 (for personal income taxpayers). While California conforms to the foundational base amount architecture of Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41(c) and provides a 15 percent regular credit rate, R&TC § 23609(i) (formerly codified at § 23609(h)(3)) and § 17052.12(h) restrict "gross receipts" strictly to sales of property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business that is delivered or shipped to a purchaser within California—explicitly excluding receipts from services, software-as-a-service (SaaS) subscriptions, royalties, licenses, rents, operating leases, interest, and throwback sales. Under California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01 (LDG 2012-03-01), taxpayers with California QREs but zero qualifying California gross receipts remain eligible for the 15 percent regular credit, but must compute their base amount using start-up rules and apply the mandatory 50 percent minimum base amount floor of I.R.C. § 41(c)(2).

Primary Congressional Research Service (CRS) and U.S. Department of the Treasury Office of Tax Analysis (OTA) models show that for a firm constrained by the 50 percent floor, the post-§ 280C(c) MER is 6.5 percent under the pre-2018 35 percent corporate tax rate (10% × (1 − 0.35)), 7.9 percent under the current 21 percent corporate tax rate in 26 U.S.C. § 11(b) (10% × (1 − 0.21)), and 8.0 percent under the CRS 20 percent basis-adjustment benchmark (10% × (1 − 0.20)), whereas 4.55 percent was Treasury OTA's undiscounted effective rate for the Alternative Simplified Credit, not the § 41(c)(2) floor. That method was repealed for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2011, by Section 301(c) of the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 (Pub. L. 112-240) and the April 3, 2015 final and temporary regulations (Federal Register Document 2015-07331); current 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-6(c) and 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1)(A)(ii) mandate allocating the group credit in direct proportion to each member's share of aggregate group QREs, regardless of stand-alone entity credits.

Official FTB Form 3523 Instructions and audit manuals explicitly prohibited zero-gross-receipts taxpayers under LDG 2012-03-01 from electing the AIC, mandating that they use the Regular Research Credit and its 50 percent minimum base amount floor. Under SB 711, California repealed only the AIC effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, while retaining the 15 percent Regular Research Credit alongside the new modified ASC (3 percent of QREs exceeding 50 percent of 3-year average QREs, or 1.3 percent if no QREs in any of the 3 prior years), and the 2025 Form FTB 3523 instructions issue no such advisory.
Architecture of the Federal Research Credit and Base Amount Formula

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a), the federal research credit is a component of the general business credit under 26 U.S.C. § 38. Specifically, 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) defines the regular research credit for a taxable year as 20 percent of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over the "base amount" (supplemented under § 41(a)(2) and (a)(3) by 20 percent of basic research payments determined under § 41(e)(1)(A) and 20 percent of amounts paid or incurred to an energy research consortium). Because the regular credit applies only to incremental QREs above the historical base amount rather than total research outlays, the statutory computation of the base amount directly governs the credit's yield.
Qualified Research Expenses Under 26 U.S.C. Section 41(b) and the Section 41(d) Four-Part Test

Before computing the base amount or testing the 50 percent floor under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2), a taxpayer must quantify its current-year QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b). Under § 41(b)(1), QREs equal the sum of in-house research expenses and contract research expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer (with § 41(b)(4) disregarding the trade or business requirement for in-house research expenses of startup ventures whose principal purpose is to use the research results in the active conduct of a future trade or business).

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), in-house research expenses are restricted to three statutory categories. First, eligible wages (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a), or earned income under § 401(c)(2) for self-employed individuals, excluding wages taken into account for the § 51(a) work opportunity credit) encompass compensation paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services"—defined in § 41(b)(2)(B) as engaging in qualified research or engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of qualified research; if "substantially all" (at least 80 percent) of an individual's services during the taxable year meet this standard, all of that individual's services for the year qualify. Second, eligible supplies under § 41(b)(2)(C) encompass any tangible property used in the conduct of qualified research other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Third, under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) includes any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers (computer rental or lease costs) in the conduct of qualified research.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3), contract research expenses generally equal 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research (§ 41(b)(3)(A)). This inclusion rate increases to 75 percent for amounts paid or incurred to a qualified research consortium—a tax-exempt organization under § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6) organized and operated primarily to conduct scientific research that is not a private foundation (§ 41(b)(3)(C))—and 100 percent for amounts paid to eligible small businesses (500 or fewer employees), institutions of higher education (§ 3304(f)), or Federal laboratories for qualified energy research (§ 41(b)(3)(D)).

To be included in QREs, the underlying activities must satisfy the four-part statutory test for "qualified research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), applied separately to each discrete business component (product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business, subject to the "shrink-back" rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)):

items: The Section 174 / Section 174A Eligibility Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A)): The expenditures must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business in the experimental or laboratory sense to eliminate uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design. While that description reflects pre-2022 law, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206) eliminated current expensing for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, requiring mandatory 5-year amortization for domestic research and 15-year amortization for foreign research under 26 U.S.C. § 174. Subsequently, Section 70302 of Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025) enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A (Domestic research or experimental expenditures) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (and before January 1, 2030), restoring immediate current deductibility (or an elective amortization period of not less than 60 months under § 174A(c)) for domestic research expenditures and amending § 41(d)(1)(A) to cross-reference § 174A, while leaving 26 U.S.C. § 174 to govern 15-year amortization of foreign research or experimental expenditures. Furthermore, § 41 remains narrower than § 174 and § 174A because expenditures such as patent procurement costs or quality control testing are excluded from § 41 QREs.

The Technological Information Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—meaning it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

The Business Component Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)): The application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer relating to function, performance, reliability, or quality (and not style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under § 41(d)(3)(B)).

The Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all—defined in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—of the research activities for the business component must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation evaluating one or more alternatives to eliminate technical uncertainty.

body.text: The Base Amount Mechanism Under 26 U.S.C. Section 41(c)(1) and (c)(2)

Once current-year QREs are established, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1) defines the taxpayer's "base amount" as the product of two statutory variables: the fixed-base percentage under § 41(c)(1)(A)—representing the historical ratio of the taxpayer's aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts during its statutory base period (or phased-in start-up schedule under § 41(c)(3))—and the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer under § 41(c)(1)(B) for the four taxable years preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined (referred to in the statute as the "credit year").
Immediately following that general formula, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) (Minimum base amount) imposes an overarching statutory floor:

As codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2): "In no event shall the base amount be less than 50 percent of the qualified research expenses for the credit year.". Consequently, no matter how small a taxpayer's fixed-base percentage or prior four-year average gross receipts may be, at least 50 percent of the current year's QREs are absorbed by the base amount, leaving at most 50 percent of current-year QREs eligible for the 20 percent federal regular credit rate.
Legislative History, Congressional Intent, and Marginal Effective Rate Analysis

The structure of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c) reflects more than four decades of legislative calibration aimed at correcting private-market underinvestment in research—caused by positive societal spillover externalities that innovating firms cannot fully capture in market prices—while preventing windfall subsidies for baseline research that firms would have conducted without tax incentives.
From ERTA 1981 to the 1989 Fixed-Base Percentage Overhaul

Congress first enacted the federal research tax credit in Section 221 of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA, Pub. L. 97-34, 95 Stat. 172, 241, enacted August 13, 1981), championed by Representative Jack Kemp and Senator William Roth and initially codified at I.R.C. § 44F (renumbered § 30 by the Deficit Reduction Act of 1984, Pub. L. 98-369, and redesignated § 41 by the Tax Reform Act of 1986, Pub. L. 99-514). Under ERTA 1981, the credit was set at a 25 percent statutory rate (reduced to 20 percent by the Tax Reform Act of 1986) on QREs exceeding "base period research expenses," which were defined as the rolling average of the taxpayer's QREs over the three immediately preceding taxable years. Notably, as the Minnesota Supreme Court later documented in General Mills, Inc. v. Commissioner of Revenue (2019), the 50 percent minimum base amount limitation was built into the federal statute from its inception under former I.R.C. § 44F(c)(3).

By the late 1980s, public finance economists, the Congressional Research Service (CRS), and the Treasury Department identified a severe structural defect in the three-year rolling average base period. Because a taxpayer's base amount in Years 2, 3, and 4 was tied directly to its QREs in Year 1, every additional dollar of research spending in Year 1 automatically increased the taxpayer's base amount by one-third of a dollar in each of the next three taxable years. This created a disincentive or "penalty effect" in which current-year credit gains were substantially offset—or even rendered negative in present-value terms—by the erosion of future credits.

To eliminate this rolling-base penalty effect, Congress overhauled the base calculation in Section 7110 of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989 (OBRA 1989, Pub. L. 101-239, 103 Stat. 2106, 2322–2325, enacted December 19, 1989). OBRA 1989 decoupled the base amount from prior-year QREs and indexed it instead to four-year average annual gross receipts multiplied by a stationary "fixed-base percentage" locked to the taxpayer's 1984–1988 ratio of QREs to gross receipts. After 16 temporary extensions since 1981, Congress made the § 41 research credit permanent in the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015.
Windfall Containment, IRC Section 280C(c), and Marginal Effective Rate Compression

While indexing the base amount to gross receipts in OBRA 1989 eliminated the rolling-base penalty on increasing QREs, it exposed the federal Treasury to potential windfall claims whenever a company's current-year research spending expanded far faster than its four-year average gross receipts, or when a start-up incurred large QREs alongside minimal early revenues. Under Section 3(3) of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974, the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) and Congressional Budget Committees evaluate the § 41 credit as a tax expenditure (revenue loss attributable to a special credit). Maintaining the 50 percent minimum base amount under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) ensures that the regular credit cannot turn into a flat 20 percent subsidy on 100 percent of a firm's research budget. According to U.S. Treasury Office of Tax Analysis (OTA) tax return data, corporate taxpayers constrained by the § 41(c)(2) 50 percent minimum base amount account for 44 percent of all corporate returns claiming the regular credit and 28 percent of total corporate research spending.

body.text: As illustrated in the rate compression analysis above, the 50 percent minimum base amount floor under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) alters the Marginal Effective Rate (MER)—defined by the Treasury OTA and CRS as the present-value reduction in tax liability resulting from a marginal $1.00 increase in current-year QREs. When an unconstrained firm's calculated base amount exceeds 50 percent of its current-year QREs (because its historical fixed-base percentage times four-year average gross receipts is higher than the 50 percent floor, while its current-year QREs still exceed that calculated base), an incremental $1.00 of QREs does not change the current year's base amount; the entire $1.00 qualifies for the 20 percent statutory credit rate, yielding $0.20 of gross credit. By contrast, when a firm's calculated base amount is less than 50 percent of its current-year QREs, § 41(c)(2) locks the base amount at 50 percent of current-year QREs. Under this binding floor, spending an additional $1.00 on QREs automatically raises the current year's minimum base amount by $0.50, leaving only $0.50 of incremental excess QREs eligible for the 20 percent rate and cutting the nominal marginal credit yield in half to 10.0 percent (0.20 × $0.50 = $0.10).

This nominal 10.0 percent marginal rate is then reduced a second time by 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c), which prevents taxpayers from claiming both a full research expense deduction (or capital account charge) and a full tax credit on the same expenditure dollar. Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) (as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(b)(2)(B), effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024), a taxpayer's domestic research or experimental expenditures under § 174A(b) otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to capital account must be reduced by 100 percent of the research credit allowed under § 41(a). Alternatively, under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(2), a taxpayer may make an irrevocable election on its timely filed original return (including extensions, via IRS Form 6765) to avoid reducing its deduction and instead claim a reduced credit equal to the § 41(a) credit minus the product of that credit and the maximum corporate tax rate under 26 U.S.C. § 11(b).

Primary CRS and Treasury OTA publications demonstrate that this 4.5 percent figure does not apply to the Regular Research Credit under § 41(c)(2). Under the pre-2018 35 percent maximum corporate tax rate, electing the reduced credit under § 280C(c) multiplied the credit by 0.65 (1 − 0.35). As documented in CRS Report RL31181 and the Treasury OTA 2016 study, this reduced the unconstrained Regular Credit MER from 20.0 percent to 13.0 percent (20% × 0.65) and reduced the 50%-floor-constrained Regular Credit MER from 10.0 percent to 6.5 percent (10% × 0.65). Even after Treasury OTA discounted the constrained regular credit by an 82 percent realization factor to account for firms carrying unused credits forward, the effective rate was 5.3 percent (and in an earlier Tax Foundation example using a 34 percent corporate tax rate, the net effective rate at the 50 percent floor was 6.6 percent).

Under the current 21 percent maximum corporate tax rate in 26 U.S.C. § 11(b), the § 280C(c)(2) reduced credit election retains 79 percent of the credit (1 − 0.21 = 0.79). Consequently, the unconstrained Regular Credit MER is 15.8 percent (20% × 0.79) and the § 41(c)(2) 50%-floor-constrained Regular Credit MER is 7.9 percent (10% × 0.79). Similarly, in the updated edition of CRS Report RL31181 (which models a 20 percent basis adjustment), the unconstrained Regular Credit MER is 16.0 percent (20% × (1 − 0.20)), the maximum ASC MER is 11.2 percent (14% × (1 − 0.20)), and the 50%-floor-constrained Regular Credit MER is 8.0 percent (10% × (1 − 0.20)). The 4.55 percent figure (or 5.0 percent when discounted at 5 percent) in Treasury OTA's analysis is the marginal effective rate of the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC)—because the 14 percent ASC reduced by 35 percent under § 280C(c) yields 9.1 percent in the current year, but raises the three-year moving average QRE base over the next three years, cutting the undiscounted 9.1 percent ASC benefit in half to 4.55 percent. (Separately, CRS Report RL31181 notes that if a firm constrained by the 50 percent floor under the pre-2018 35 percent corporate rate invests in an R&D project where non-creditable physical capital/equipment makes up 50 percent of total project costs, the effective subsidy across total project costs drops from 6.5 percent to 3.25 percent).
Mathematical Mechanics of the 50 Percent Floor and Start-Up Provisions
Applying 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) requires executing a three-step statutory test that compares the gross-receipts-based baseline under § 41(c)(1) and (c)(3) against half of current-year QREs.
The Section 41(c)(1)–(3) Comparison Test and 16 Percent Cap

For an established taxpayer—one that had both gross receipts and QREs in at least three taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (the 1984–1988 base period)—26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(A) defines the Fixed-Base Percentage (FBP) as the ratio of the taxpayer's aggregate QREs for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, to its aggregate gross receipts for those same taxable years. Two statutory rules bound this ratio: under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C) (Maximum fixed-base percentage), "In no event shall the fixed-base percentage exceed 16 percent," and under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(D) (Rounding), the fixed-base percentage determined under subparagraph (A) or (B)(ii) must be rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1 percent (two decimal places, such as 6.25 percent).
Once the FBP is established, the taxpayer performs the three-step comparison required by 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1) and (c)(2):

items: Step 1 (Calculated Base Amount under § 41(c)(1)): Multiply the Fixed-Base Percentage (capped at 16.00%) by the Average Annual Gross Receipts (AAGR) for the four taxable years immediately preceding the credit year.
Step 2 (Minimum Base Amount Floor under § 41(c)(2)): Multiply current-year QREs by 50 percent (0.50 × Current-Year QREs).
Step 3 (Applicable Base Amount): Select the greater of Step 1 or Step 2.

body.text: Mathematically, the 50 percent minimum base amount floor in Step 2 is triggered whenever:

Thus, as CRS Report RL31181 confirms, whenever a taxpayer's current-year research intensity (the ratio of current-year QREs to prior four-year average annual gross receipts) is more than double its historical fixed-base percentage (or exceeds 32 percent of prior four-year AAGR for a firm at the 16 percent FBP cap), the taxpayer is automatically bound by the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of § 41(c)(2).
Start-Up Company Rules Under Section 41(c)(3)(B) and Division-by-Zero Defaults

To accommodate businesses formed after the 1984–1988 historical window or lacking sufficient base-period activity, Congress enacted special start-up rules in 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B) (originally added for post-1988 firms and expanded by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993, Pub. L. 103-66, and Section 1204 of the Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996, Pub. L. 104-188). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i), a taxpayer is classified as a "start-up company" if either (I) the first taxable year in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs begins after December 31, 1983, or (II) there are fewer than three taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs.

body.text: Inspection of the statutory text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(I)–(VII) shows that the transition phase spans five years (Years 6 through 10), does not blend the 3 percent rate into Years 6–10, and reaches full historical maturity in Year 11. Specifically, under § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(I), the FBP is fixed at 3 percent (0.03) for each of the taxpayer's first five taxable years beginning after December 31, 1993, for which the taxpayer has QREs. Thereafter, the FBP is computed as 1/6 of the aggregate QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio of the 4th and 5th such taxable years in the 6th such year (§ 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(II)); 1/3 of the aggregate ratio of the 5th and 6th such years in the 7th such year (§ 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(III)); 1/2 of the aggregate ratio of the 5th, 6th, and 7th such years in the 8th such year (§ 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(IV)); 2/3 of the aggregate ratio of the 5th through 8th such years in the 9th such year (§ 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(V)); and 5/6 of the aggregate ratio of the 5th through 9th such years in the 10th such year (§ 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(VI)). In the 11th such taxable year and all subsequent years (§ 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(VII)), the FBP equals 100 percent of the aggregate QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio for any five taxable years selected by the taxpayer from among the 5th through the 10th such taxable years, subject to the 16 percent maximum cap of § 41(c)(3)(C).

Crucially, the 50 percent minimum base amount floor under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) applies equally to start-up companies and established firms. Because a start-up's FBP is set at 3 percent during its first five post-1993 QRE years, any start-up whose current-year QREs exceed 6 percent (2 × 3%) of its prior four-year average annual gross receipts will have a calculated base amount below 50 percent of current-year QREs and will automatically trigger the § 41(c)(2) 50 percent floor. Furthermore, as documented in FTB Form 3523 instructions and the FTB S-Corporation Manual, if a start-up (or a California taxpayer treated as a start-up under LDG 2012-03-01) has $0 gross receipts in its 6th year and beyond, computing the historical ratio requires dividing by zero, which creates a mathematical error; in that event, the statutory cap in 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C) controls and the taxpayer must enter the maximum fixed-base percentage of 16 percent (0.16). Multiplying that 16 percent FBP by $0 average annual gross receipts still produces a calculated base amount of $0, which immediately engages the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2).
Advanced Corporate Structures: Controlled Groups and Acquisitions

In multi-entity corporate enterprises and post-merger structures, 26 U.S.C. § 41(f) prevents taxpayers from circumventing the 50 percent minimum base amount floor by isolating research activities in low-revenue subsidiaries or acquiring research-intensive businesses without their historical revenue baselines.
Controlled Group Aggregation and Allocation Under Section 41(f)(1) and Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-6

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1)(A)(i) and (B)(i) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-6(b)(1), all members of a controlled group of corporations (as defined in § 41(f)(5), referencing § 1563(a) with a "more than 50 percent" common ownership threshold substituted for "at least 80 percent") and all trades or businesses under common control (under 26 C.F.R. § 1.52-1(b)–(g)) are treated as a single taxpayer for purposes of computing the research credit. All members of the controlled group must use the same computation method for the credit year. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-6(i)(1), because the group is treated as a single taxpayer, intra-group transfers between members are generally disregarded in determining both QREs and gross receipts (subject to a narrow regulatory exception proposed in Federal Register Document 2013-29539 on December 13, 2013, where an intra-group transfer is followed by a foreign corporate member's external sale that does not generate U.S. effectively connected gross receipts under § 41(c)(6) [formerly § 41(c)(7)]).

When computing the "group credit" under the regular method, all computational rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41—including the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of § 41(c)(2)—are applied on an aggregate group-wide basis. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-6(b)(2), a controlled group is treated as a start-up company under § 41(c)(3)(B)(i) only if there was no taxable year beginning before January 1, 1984, in which a member had gross receipts and the same or another member had QREs, or if there were fewer than three taxable years between 1984 and 1988 in which a member had gross receipts and the same or another member had QREs (with the group's first post-1993 QRE year defined as the first year in which at least one member has QREs). The group's FBP is the ratio of the group's aggregate 1984–1988 QREs to the group's aggregate 1984–1988 gross receipts (or the group start-up FBP), capped at 16 percent. The group's minimum base amount under § 41(c)(2) equals 50 percent of the group's aggregate credit-year QREs, and the group's applicable base amount is the greater of the group FBP multiplied by the group's aggregate four-year average annual gross receipts or the group's 50 percent minimum base amount.

That assertion relies on the 2003 proposed regulations (Federal Register Document 03-17870, July 29, 2003) and pre-2012 versions of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6(c), which are no longer in force. In Section 301(c) of the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 (Pub. L. 112-240, H.R. 8), Congress amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1)(A)(ii) and § 41(f)(1)(B)(ii) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2011, to mandate that the group credit be allocated to each controlled group member "on a proportionate basis to its share of the aggregate of the qualified research expenses, basic research payments, and amounts paid or incurred to energy research consortiums, taken into account by such controlled group for purposes of this section.". As confirmed in IRS Notice 2013-20, the April 3, 2015 final and temporary regulations (Federal Register Document 2015-07331), and the current text of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-6(c) (current as of November 5, 2026), the stand-alone entity credit method was eliminated. Today, the group credit is allocated to each member strictly in proportion to that member's share of the controlled group's aggregate QREs (plus basic research payments and energy research consortium amounts, if any) for the taxable year, without regard to whether the member would have a stand-alone entity credit or what the amount of any such credit would be:

Furthermore, under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-6(d)(1) and (d)(3), members of a consolidated group that belong to a broader controlled group are treated as a single member for initial controlled-group allocation, and the consolidated group's share is then sub-allocated among its consolidated members in proportion to each consolidated member's share of the consolidated group's QREs. (In California, the FTB Multistate Audit Technical Manual confirms that California applied the stand-alone entity credit method only for taxable years ending May 24, 2005 through December 31, 2014, and conformed to the federal proportionate QRE expenditure allocation method for taxable years ending after December 31, 2014).
Mergers, Acquisitions, and Predecessor Adjustments Under Section 41(f)(3)

When a taxpayer acquires or disposes of the major portion of a trade or business—or the major portion of a separate unit thereof (defined in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(b) by cross-reference to 26 C.F.R. § 1.52-2(b) as a viable trade or business that can be operated independently, including an incorporation or a liquidation)—26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(A) and (B) (as amended by Section 301(b) of the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012, Pub. L. 112-240) mandate symmetrical adjustments to historical QREs and gross receipts during the "measurement period" so that the research credit is computed consistently before and after the transaction. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(A)(vi), the term "measurement period" means, with respect to the taxable year of the acquiring person for which the credit is determined, any period of the acquiring person preceding such taxable year which is taken into account for purposes of determining the credit for such year.

Specifically, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(A)(i)–(iii) (Acquisitions), if a person acquires the major portion of either a trade or business or a separate unit of a trade or business ("acquired business") of another person ("predecessor"), the acquiring person's QREs and gross receipts during the measurement period are increased under two distinct temporal rules. For any taxable year after the taxable year in which the acquisition is made (§ 41(f)(3)(A)(ii)(II) and (iii)), the acquiring person's measurement-period QREs and gross receipts are increased by 100 percent of the QREs paid or incurred by, and the gross receipts of, the predecessor with respect to the acquired business during the measurement period. For the taxable year in which the acquisition is made (§ 41(f)(3)(A)(ii)(I), (iii), and (iv)), the acquiring person's measurement-period QREs and gross receipts are increased by the "acquisition year amount"—defined in § 41(f)(3)(A)(iv) as the product of (I) the QREs paid or incurred by (or gross receipts of) the predecessor with respect to the acquired business during the measurement period, and (II) the number of days in the period beginning on the date of the acquisition and ending on the last day of the taxable year in which the acquisition is made, divided by the number of days in the acquiring person's taxable year:

In the case of an acquiring person and a predecessor whose taxable years do not begin on the same date, 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(A)(v)(I)–(IV) establishes special rules for coordinating taxable years: (I) each reference to a taxable year in clauses (ii) and (iv) refers to the appropriate taxable year of the acquiring person; (II) the QREs paid or incurred by the predecessor, and the gross receipts of the predecessor, during each taxable year of the predecessor any portion of which is part of the measurement period shall be allocated equally among the days of such taxable year; and (III)–(IV) the amount of such QREs and gross receipts taken into account with respect to a taxable year of the acquiring person equals the total of the expenses or gross receipts attributable under subclause (II) to the days occurring during such taxable year.

Conversely, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(B) (Dispositions), if the predecessor furnishes to the acquiring person such information as is necessary for the application of subparagraph (A), then for any taxable year ending after the disposition, the disposing predecessor's measurement-period QREs and gross receipts are reduced by: (i) in the taxable year in which the disposition is made, the predecessor's measurement-period QREs and gross receipts attributable to the acquired business multiplied by the number of days from the acquisition date to the last day of the predecessor's taxable year of disposition, divided by the number of days in the predecessor's taxable year; and (ii) in any taxable year ending after the disposition year, 100 percent of those attributable measurement-period QREs and gross receipts. Furthermore, under § 41(f)(3)(C), if during any of the three taxable years following the disposition year the disposing taxpayer (or a person required to aggregate expenditures with it under paragraph (1)) reimburses the acquiring person (or a person required to aggregate expenditures with it) for research on behalf of the taxpayer, the disposing taxpayer's QREs for the taxable years taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage are increased by the lesser of the subparagraph (B) decrease allocable to those base-period years or the product of the number of such years multiplied by the reimbursement. In practice, when an established corporation acquires a research-intensive, pre-revenue start-up, adding the target's substantial current-year QREs to the acquirer's QRE pool while adding little or no historical gross receipts frequently pushes the combined enterprise's QREs above twice its adjusted base-period ratio, triggering the 50 percent minimum base amount floor under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2).
State Conformity and Divergence: The California R&TC Section 23609 Framework

The interaction between 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) and state tax conformity is nowhere more pronounced than in California, which administers its Research Credit under Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) § 23609 (for Corporation Tax Law filers) and R&TC § 17052.12 (for Personal Income Tax Law filers) via Form FTB 3523 (Research Credit). For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2000, both R&TC § 23609(b)(3) and § 17052.12(b)(3) modify the 20 percent federal regular credit rate in I.R.C. § 41(a)(1) to 15 percent of the excess of California QREs over the base amount (while § 23609(b)(3) also provides corporations—other than S-corporations, personal holding companies, and service organizations—a 24 percent credit on basic research payments made in cash under a written contract to qualified universities, scientific research organizations, or qualifying cancer/biotechnology centers in California). Unused California research credits cannot be carried back, but carry over indefinitely to offset future tax liabilities in the earliest possible taxable year under R&TC § 23609(f) and § 17052.12(e).
In-State Geographic Nexus and the Narrow Definition of California Gross Receipts

While California incorporates the base amount framework of I.R.C. § 41(c)—including the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of I.R.C. § 41(c)(2)—it enforces two state-specific statutory modifications that substantially alter the base amount calculation. First, under R&TC § 23609(c)(2) and § 17052.12(d), "Qualified research" and "basic research" shall include only research conducted in California. Multistate taxpayers must segregate their federal QREs so that only wages for qualified services performed physically within California, supplies used in California research activities (excluding tangible personal property eligible for the R&TC § 6378 sales and use tax exemption under § 23609(c)(1)), and contract research performed within California enter the California QRE pool.

Second, California imposes a highly restrictive definition of gross receipts under R&TC § 23609(i) (formerly codified at § 23609(h)(3)) and § 17052.12(h). Under federal law (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-3(c) and 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6)), gross receipts broadly encompass total revenues from all activities and sources under the taxpayer's accounting method (reduced by returns and allowances). By contrast, R&TC § 23609(i) and § 17052.12(h) modify I.R.C. § 41(c)(6) to take into account "only those gross receipts from the sale of property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of the taxpayer's trade or business that is delivered or shipped to a purchaser within this state, regardless of f.o.b. point or any other condition of the sale.".

Crucially, the FTB Form 3523 Instructions explicitly state that receipts from services (including consulting, custom engineering, and Software-as-a-Service [SaaS] subscriptions classified as services), rents, operating leases, interest, royalties, licenses (such as software licensing fees or pharmaceutical patent out-licensing), and throwback sales (sales shipped from California to purchasers in other states where the taxpayer is not taxable, which are "thrown back" to California for general corporate income tax sales-factor apportionment) are excluded from the California R&D gross receipts computation. Because of these exclusions, a California software, SaaS, engineering services, or biotechnology enterprise can generate billions of dollars in global service, subscription, or licensing revenue while recording $0 in qualifying California gross receipts under R&TC § 23609(i).
FTB Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01 and Mandatory Floor Application

When a taxpayer's four-year average annual California gross receipts equal $0, multiplying any fixed-base percentage by $0 yields a calculated base amount of $0 under I.R.C. § 41(c)(1). Prior to 2012, the California Franchise Tax Board initially took the position (in withdrawn LDG 2011-06-01) that a purely service-based company with $0 qualifying gross receipts under R&TC § 23609 could not claim the California Regular Research Credit at all. Following taxpayer challenges, the FTB issued Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01 (LDG 2012-03-01) on March 1, 2012.

LDG 2012-03-01—codified directly into the Specific Line Instructions for Form FTB 3523 (Lines 10 and 11) and FTB audit manuals—establishes three mandatory rules for any taxpayer with California QREs but no California gross receipts:

items: Mandatory Start-Up Fixed-Base Percentage Methodology (Line 10): Regardless of the company's actual chronological age or federal established-firm status, a taxpayer with no California gross receipts under LDG 2012-03-01 must calculate its fixed-base percentage as a start-up company, treating as "year one" the first taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 1994, in which the taxpayer had California QREs (3 percent for Years 1–5). In the taxpayer's 6th year and beyond, because dividing by $0 California gross receipts is mathematically impossible, the statutory cap of I.R.C. § 41(c)(3)(C) controls and the taxpayer must enter the maximum fixed-base percentage of 16 percent (0.16) on Line 10.

Reporting $0 Prior Four-Year Average Gross Receipts (Line 11): If the taxpayer has no California gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years under LDG 2012-03-01, it enters $0 on Line 11 of Form FTB 3523.

Mandatory 50 Percent Minimum Base Amount Floor (I.R.C. § 41(c)(2)): Because multiplying the start-up FBP (3 percent or 16 percent) by $0 average California gross receipts yields a $0 calculated base amount, LDG 2012-03-01 and the Form FTB 3523 instructions mandate that the taxpayer compute its base amount using the minimum base amount of 50 percent of current-year California QREs pursuant to I.R.C. § 41(c)(2).

body.text: Judicial and Administrative Precedent on the Minimum Base Amount

Litigation at both the federal and state levels has repeatedly tested the boundaries of the base amount calculation, the consistency requirement, the eligibility of underlying QREs, and whether state conformity statutes incorporate the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2).
Federal Case Law: The Consistency Requirement and QRE Substantiation

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A), notwithstanding whether the statute of limitations for assessments or refunds has expired for any base-period year, the QREs (and under IRS Audit Techniques Guide principles, the gross receipts) taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs and gross receipts for the current credit year.

In Research, Inc. v. United States, 95-1 USTC ¶ 50,407 (D. Minn. 1995), the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota denied the taxpayer's research credit claim because the taxpayer included expenses from "special system projects" in its credit-year QREs and admitted incurring the same type of expenses during its base period, but had destroyed the base-period documentation and could not quantify the base-period amounts. The court held that the relative increase in QREs cannot be measured without consistently including the same project expense categories in both the base period and the credit year. Notably, the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) on the consistency requirement instructs examiners to exercise risk analysis before auditing base-period records: if a taxpayer's credit-year QREs are so large relative to gross receipts that the taxpayer is already constrained by the 50 percent minimum base amount limitation under § 41(c)(2), an upward audit adjustment to the 1984–1988 fixed-base percentage will have little or no effect on the allowable credit.

Federal courts also strictly police whether claimed expenditures satisfy the § 41(d) four-part test and § 41(b) QRE rules before they can enter the base amount and 50 percent floor computation. In Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Tax Court and Second Circuit drew a sharp distinction under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) between product research (aimed at improving the product itself) and process research (testing a new manufacturing process to produce the same product at lower cost or higher yield), holding that for process research, raw materials and ordinary production costs that the taxpayer would have incurred anyway to manufacture goods for sale are routine production expenses rather than QREs.

Similarly, in J.G. Boswell Co. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, No. 2408-19 (U.S. Tax Ct. order issued July 12, 2022; post-trial briefing ongoing as of May 2026), a California agricultural producer conducted 55 agronomic research trials (33 in 2013 and 22 in 2014) across 7 percent of its farmland ("research acres") and claimed $17,062,147 in 2014 QREs ($1,735,424 credit), which the IRS reduced to $885,132 in QREs ($117,722 credit). Denying cross-motions for summary judgment, the Tax Court agreed with Union Carbide that ordinary cultivation costs for process-only trials do not qualify as QREs, but held that if a trial seeks to develop an improved crop product (analogous to a "pilot model" under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(4)), trial cultivation costs may qualify as QREs if the § 41(d) four-part test is met; in post-trial briefing, the taxpayer has argued that after the Supreme Court overruled Chevron deference in Loper Bright, the Second Circuit's deference to the IRS in Union Carbide should no longer govern. Most recently, in George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10 (Feb. 3, 2026), involving a large integrated poultry producer, the Tax Court disallowed claimed credits for routine farming and vaccination trials reconstructed after the fact by a tax consultant—asking "Which came first, the research or the research credit study?"—and reaffirmed that taxpayers must maintain contemporaneous documentation of a planned, scientific process of experimentation and exclude ordinary production costs under Union Carbide.
State Supreme Court Jurisprudence: General Mills and IBM

While California enforces the 50 percent minimum base amount administratively via R&TC § 23609 and FTB LDG 2012-03-01, leading appellate judicial precedent on how state research credit statutes incorporate 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) was established by the Minnesota Tax Court and the Minnesota Supreme Court in General Mills, Inc. v. Commissioner of Revenue (Minn. 2019), affirming the Minnesota Tax Court's summary judgment order (Aug. 17, 2018), and International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner of Revenue, No. A18-1740 (Minn. July 31, 2019), affirming Int'l Bus. Mach. Corp. v. Comm'r of Revenue, No. 9053-R, 2018 WL 4054529 (Minn. Tax Ct. Aug. 17, 2018).

Minnesota's R&D credit statute, Minn. Stat. § 290.068, subd. 2(c), defines "base amount" as "base amount as defined in section 41(c) of the Internal Revenue Code" (with Minnesota QREs and Minnesota-sourced prior four-year average annual gross receipts). In General Mills, the taxpayer argued that the statutory phrase "as defined in" incorporated only paragraph (1) of I.R.C. § 41(c) (because § 41(c)(1) uses the word "means" to state the product of the fixed-base percentage and four-year average annual gross receipts) and excluded paragraph (2) (the 50 percent minimum base amount limitation of § 41(c)(2)).

Both the Minnesota Tax Court and the Minnesota Supreme Court rejected that argument and held that Minn. Stat. § 290.068, subd. 2(c) incorporates the 50 percent minimum base amount limitation of I.R.C. § 41(c)(2) in full. First, the court explained that reading Minn. Stat. § 290.068, subd. 2(c) to incorporate only § 41(c)(1) would render "base amount" meaningless because § 41(c)(1) depends directly on the companion paragraphs of § 41(c)—including § 41(c)(2) (minimum base amount), § 41(c)(3) (fixed-base percentage), and the consistency and gross receipts rules. Second, turning to legislative history, the court noted that when Minnesota first adopted the federal base amount concept in 1982 (referencing former I.R.C. § 44F(c)), the 50 percent floor was already embedded in § 44F(c)(3); and when Minnesota updated § 290.068 in 1991 to reference "section 41(c)," federal § 41(c) contained only provisions defining the boundaries of the base amount, whereas the optional AIC and ASC elections in paragraphs (4) and (5) were added by Congress later in 1996 and 2006.

In the companion case International Business Machines Corp. v. Commissioner of Revenue (No. A18-1740, July 31, 2019), IBM similarly cross-appealed the Tax Court's August 17, 2018 summary judgment order holding that Minn. Stat. § 290.068, subd. 2(c) incorporates the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of I.R.C. § 41(c)(2). Following General Mills, the Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed that IBM's state base amount could not fall below 50 percent of its current-year Minnesota QREs under I.R.C. § 41(c)(2).
California Office of Tax Appeals: Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation Subsidiaries

In California, the interplay between R&TC § 23609 gross receipts, FTB LDG 2012-03-01, and the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of I.R.C. § 41(c)(2) was examined by the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) in Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation Subsidiaries, OTA Case Nos. 19014166, 19125644, and 22039829 (Opinion issued September 20, 2023, following the June 14, 2023 oral hearing).

In that appeal, Electronic Data Systems (EDS) sought refunds for the 2003 through 2008 tax years totaling $35,227,616 across multiple claims. EDS initially asserted that it had $0 in California research gross receipts under R&TC § 23609(h)(3) (now § 23609(i))—arguing that § 23609(h)(3) excluded sales of intangible property and that it had no California sales of tangible personal property—and therefore sought to compute its California Regular Research Credit using the 50 percent minimum base amount floor under FTB LDG 2012-03-01 without reference to a base period. However, in June 2022, during the pendency of the OTA appeal, EDS conceded that it did have nonzero California research gross receipts, rendering the zero-gross-receipts methodology of LDG 2012-03-01 inapplicable.

Once LDG 2012-03-01 no longer applied, EDS bore the burden of substantiating its actual California gross receipts and four-year Average Annual Gross Receipts (AAGRs) to demonstrate that its California QREs exceeded its calculated base amounts under I.R.C. § 41(c)(1). Although the OTA agreed that EDS's original return method (multiplying total net gross receipts by its California sales apportionment percentage) was legally incorrect, the OTA found that EDS's revised "potential" gross receipts schedules failed to explain or substantiate which revenue streams (such as software sales versus software licensing) were included or excluded. Because EDS's total gross receipts exceeded $10 billion annually, the OTA observed that even a tiny percentage of qualifying California gross receipts would generate four-year AAGRs and calculated base amounts large enough to exceed the 50 percent minimum base amount floor and completely eliminate EDS's California QREs; accordingly, the OTA denied the refund claims.
Alternative Credit Methodologies and the 2025 California ASC Transition

Because both high-revenue firms (whose large four-year average gross receipts inflate their calculated base amount under § 41(c)(1)) and zero-gross-receipts firms (whose base amount is locked at 50 percent of current-year QREs under § 41(c)(2)) face structural constraints under the Regular Research Credit, federal and California tax laws have provided alternative elective credit methodologies.
The Pre-2025 California Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC) and the Zero-Gross-Receipts Prohibition

At the federal level, Congress enacted the Alternative Incremental Research Credit (AIRC or AIC) under former I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) in the Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-188, § 1204) for taxable years beginning after June 30, 1996, and later terminated the federal AIC for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2008. Under R&TC § 23609(h)(1) and § 17052.12(g)(1), California continued to conform to the former federal AIC (as in effect on January 1, 2015) for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025, with modified state credit rates across three tiers of the taxpayer's four-year average annual California gross receipts: 1.49 percent on QREs exceeding 1.0 percent up to 1.5 percent of four-year average annual gross receipts (Tier 1, R&TC § 23609(h)(1)(A)(i)); 1.98 percent on QREs exceeding 1.5 percent up to 2.0 percent of four-year average annual gross receipts (Tier 2, R&TC § 23609(h)(1)(A)(ii)); and 2.48 percent on QREs exceeding 2.0 percent of four-year average annual gross receipts (Tier 3, R&TC § 23609(h)(1)(A)(iii)).

The FTB Form 3523 Instructions, the FTB S-Corporation Manual (Chapter 12), and the FTB Multistate Audit Technical Manual (Chapter 9000) explicitly prohibit taxpayers with zero California gross receipts from electing or claiming the AIC: "If you have no California gross receipts (under LDG 2012-03-01), you cannot use the Alternative Incremental Credit; you must use the regular incremental credit as a start-up under Section A.".

Furthermore, even if a hypothetical taxpayer had $1 of California gross receipts, the Regular Research Credit under the 50 percent floor yields 7.50 percent of total current-year QREs (15% × 50%), which is more than three times larger than the maximum 2.48 percent AIC rate on 100 percent of QREs. Thus, the pre-2025 California AIC was never an advantage for zero-gross-receipts taxpayers; rather, it was designed for companies with large positive California gross receipts and low research-to-revenue ratios (where QREs were between 1 percent and 4 percent of California gross receipts) whose high fixed-base percentage or revenue volume eliminated their Regular Research Credit.
The 2025 Transition to the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Under SB 711

For nearly two decades after Congress enacted the federal Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) in 2006 (currently codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4), formerly § 41(c)(5)), California refused to conform to the ASC. Under the federal ASC (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A)–(B)), a taxpayer may elect a credit equal to 14 percent of current-year QREs that exceed 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years—or, if the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years, a flat 6 percent of current-year QREs.

In Senate Bill 711 (SB 711, Chapter 231, Statutes of 2025, approved by the Governor and chaptered October 1, 2025), the California Legislature amended R&TC § 23609(h) and § 17052.12(g) to overhaul California's alternative research credit regime for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025. First, under R&TC § 23609(h)(1) and § 17052.12(g)(1), the California AIC applies only to taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025, and is repealed for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025. Second, under R&TC § 23609(h)(2) and § 17052.12(g)(2), for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, California conforms to the federal ASC in I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) with modified state rates: the federal 14 percent rate in I.R.C. § 41(c)(4)(A) is modified to 3 percent (0.03) of current-year California QREs that exceed 50 percent of the average California QREs for the three preceding taxable years (R&TC § 23609(h)(2)(A)(i) and § 17052.12(g)(2)(A)(i)), and the federal 6 percent rate in I.R.C. § 41(c)(4)(B)(ii) is modified to 1.3 percent (0.013) of current-year California QREs if the taxpayer has no California QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years (R&TC § 23609(h)(2)(A)(ii) and § 17052.12(g)(2)(A)(ii)). Under R&TC § 23609(h)(2)(B), the ASC election must be made on Section B of Form FTB 3523 on a timely filed original tax return for the taxable year and applies to all subsequent taxable years unless revoked with the FTB's consent (requested via federal Form 3115 or Form 1128; deemed consent does not apply).

In reality, SB 711 phased out only the AIC. Both R&TC § 23609(b)(3) and § 17052.12(b)(3) and the 2025 Instructions for Form FTB 3523 retain the 15 percent Regular Research Credit (Section A) in full force alongside the new Alternative Simplified Credit (Section B). As the 2025 Form FTB 3523 instructions state: "Taxpayers who previously elected the AIC must elect either the regular credit (Section A) or the ASC (Section B) for taxable years beginning January 1, 2025, by filing form FTB 3523. A previous AIC election will not default to either credit.".

Furthermore, from a mathematical standpoint, a taxpayer with $0 California gross receipts claiming the Regular Research Credit under LDG 2012-03-01 and the § 41(c)(2) 50 percent floor receives a credit equal to 7.50 percent of its current-year California QREs (15% × (100% − 50%)), whereas electing the California ASC yields less than 3.00 percent of current-year QREs (or 1.30 percent if it lacked QREs in any of the prior three years). Thus, the 2025 California ASC is advantageous for taxpayers with positive California gross receipts whose calculated base amount under § 41(c)(1) eliminates or severely restricts their Regular Research Credit—not for $0 gross-receipts taxpayers, who achieve a much higher credit under the Regular Credit's 50 percent floor.
Hypothetical Worked Computations, Pass-Through Allocations, and Method Comparison
Hypothetical Scenario 1: Established Manufacturing Firm (Floor Not Triggered)

Assume a hypothetical California manufacturing corporation ("Established Corp") sells physical equipment delivered to customers inside California and incurs moderate R&D growth during the credit year, recording $500,000 in current-year California QREs, $5,000,000 in prior four-year average annual California gross receipts, a 6.00% (0.06) historical fixed-base percentage, and a 15.0% (0.15) California Regular Research Credit (RRC) rate:

items: Step 1 — Compute Standard Calculated Base Amount (I.R.C. § 41(c)(1)): Multiplying the 6.00% fixed-base percentage by $5,000,000 in prior four-year average California gross receipts yields a calculated base amount of $300,000 (0.06 × $5,000,000 = $300,000).

Step 2 — Compute Statutory Minimum Base Amount Floor (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2)): Multiplying current-year California QREs of $500,000 by 50.0% yields a minimum base amount floor of $250,000 (0.50 × $500,000 = $250,000).

Step 3 — Determine Applicable Base Amount: Selecting the greater of Step 1 ($300,000) or Step 2 ($250,000) establishes an applicable base amount of $300,000. Because the company's current-year QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio (10.0% = $500,000 / $5,000,000) does not exceed twice its fixed-base percentage (2 × 6.00% = 12.00%), the 50 percent minimum base amount floor of § 41(c)(2) is not triggered.

Step 4 — Compute Excess QREs and Gross California Regular Research Credit: Subtracting the $300,000 applicable base amount from $500,000 of current-year QREs leaves $200,000 in excess QREs ($500,000 − $300,000 = $200,000), which multiplied by the 15.0% California RRC rate yields a total California Regular Research Credit of $30,000 ($200,000 × 15.0% = $30,000), representing an effective credit yield of 6.00% ($30,000 / $500,000) on total current-year California QREs before any § 280C(c) reduction.

body.text: Hypothetical Scenario 2: California SaaS Firm With Zero Qualifying Gross Receipts (50 Percent Floor Triggered)

Assume a hypothetical California software enterprise ("SaaS Corp") in its 7th taxable year generates $50,000,000 in global revenue exclusively from cloud software subscriptions (services) and software licensing fees. Because services, royalties, and licenses are excluded from California gross receipts under R&TC § 23609(i) and Form FTB 3523 instructions, SaaS Corp has $0 in prior four-year average annual California gross receipts (Line 11), $2,000,000 in current-year California QREs, a 16.00% (0.16) statutory default fixed-base percentage (in Year 6+ under I.R.C. § 41(c)(3)(C) and LDG 2012-03-01, Line 10), and a 15.0% (0.15) California RRC rate:

items: Step 1 — Compute Standard Calculated Base Amount (I.R.C. § 41(c)(1)): Multiplying the 16.00% default fixed-base percentage by $0 in prior four-year average California gross receipts yields a calculated base amount of $0 (0.16 × $0 = $0).

Step 2 — Compute Statutory Minimum Base Amount Floor (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) & LDG 2012-03-01): Multiplying current-year California QREs of $2,000,000 by 50.0% yields a minimum base amount floor of $1,000,000 (0.50 × $2,000,000 = $1,000,000).

Step 3 — Determine Applicable Base Amount: Selecting the greater of Step 1 ($0) or Step 2 ($1,000,000) establishes an applicable base amount of $1,000,000, as FTB LDG 2012-03-01 and 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) override the $0 calculated base amount and impose the mandatory 50 percent floor.

Step 4 — Compute Excess QREs and Gross California Regular Research Credit: Subtracting the $1,000,000 applicable base amount from $2,000,000 of current-year QREs leaves $1,000,000 in excess QREs ($2,000,000 − $1,000,000 = $1,000,000), which multiplied by the 15.0% California RRC rate yields a total California Regular Research Credit of $150,000 ($1,000,000 × 15.0% = $150,000). Without the 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) floor, a $0 base amount would have produced a $300,000 credit ($2,000,000 × 15.0%); the 50 percent floor neutralizes $1,000,000 of QREs and halves the gross credit to $150,000 (7.50% of total current-year QREs). By comparison, if SaaS Corp instead elected the new 2025 California ASC (assuming prior three-year average California QREs of $1,500,000, so the 50% historical QRE base is $750,000), its ASC would be $37,500 (($2,000,000 − $750,000) × 3.0%), or $26,000 ($2,000,000 × 1.3%) if it lacked QREs in any of the prior three years—demonstrating why a $0 gross-receipts taxpayer obtains a much larger credit ($150,000) by remaining on the Regular Research Credit despite the 50 percent floor.

body.text: S-Corporation and Pass-Through Entity Credit Limitations

When a taxpayer subject to the 50 percent minimum base amount floor operates as a pass-through entity (an S-corporation, partnership, or LLC taxed as a partnership), additional statutory reductions and utilization caps apply after the entity computes its gross credit on Form FTB 3523. First, unlike federal tax law (where 100 percent of an S-corporation's research credit passes through to shareholders under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(a)(1)(i) and I.R.C. §§ 1366 and 1377), California imposes a 1.5 percent entity-level tax on S-corporations (3.5 percent for financial S-corporations). Under R&TC § 23803(a)(1), an S-corporation may claim only one-third (1/3) of the research credit computed on Form FTB 3523 against its 1.5 percent entity-level tax; the remaining two-thirds (2/3) is permanently disregarded at the corporate level and cannot be carried over or passed through. Concurrently, under the Personal Income Tax Law (R&TC § 23803(a)(2)(F)), the S-corporation passes through 100 percent of the computed research credit pro rata to its shareholders on Schedule K-1 (100S). (If a C-corporation with unused research credit carryovers converts to an S-corporation, its carryovers are reduced to 1/3 upon election and cannot be passed through to shareholders). In the case of a partnership, under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(a)(3)(i), because the research credit is an expenditure-based credit, the credit is allocated among partners in the same proportion as § 174 / § 174A research expenditures are allocated for the year under I.R.C. § 704 and 26 C.F.R. § 1.704-1(b)(4)(ii).

Second, under R&TC § 24440 and the Form FTB 3523 instructions, unless a taxpayer elects the reduced credit under I.R.C. § 280C(c), it must reduce its state research expense deduction (add back the full credit generated to California taxable income). Pass-through entities report the unreduced distributive share of the credit on Schedule K-1 (Form 100S, 541, 565, or 568) and instruct recipients in the "Other Information" section to multiply the credit by their applicable California § 280C(c) credit reduction percentage (which equals 1 minus the maximum California tax rate for that taxpayer class): 98.5% (0.985) for S-corporations (reflecting the 1.5% entity-level tax rate), 91.16% (0.9116) for C-corporations (reflecting the 8.84% corporate tax rate), and 87.7% (0.877) for individuals, estates, and trusts (reflecting the 12.3% top regular personal income tax rate).

Third, under I.R.C. § 41(g) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(c) (as modified by R&TC § 23609(k) and § 17052.12(j)), pass-through research credits received by an individual, partner, LLC member, estate/trust beneficiary, or S-corporation shareholder cannot exceed the amount of net income tax attributable to that person's taxable income from that specific business interest:

Excess credits disallowed by § 41(g) in the current year carry over indefinitely to subsequent taxable years, subject to the § 41(g) limitation in each carryover year (and under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(d), the taxpayer to whom the credit was passed through is not prevented from applying the unused carryover merely because the entity that earned the credit changes its form of conducting business). Finally, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, total business credits (including the research credit and carryovers) may not reduce corporate "tax" or personal "net tax" by more than $5,000,000 per year (applied at the combined reporting group level), with carryover periods extended by the number of years a credit is disallowed.
